$comment: One seat = one audience. This is the illustrative Retail seat - and the shape to copy. To add an audience, copy it to council/<your-audience>.json (a NEW name) and rewrite it for them, keeping a DIFFERENT outcome from the other seats so the room can disagree. THE #1 RULE: every criterion must be one that ANOTHER audience would score differently - a bar that scores the same for any reader is generic writing quality (the solo critic's job, not a seat's), so cut it. That disagreement is the entire point. Each field below carries its own note; when you ask Copilot or Cowork to draft a seat, give it the real audience and their constraints and keep every criterion tied to THIS audience's outcome. (All keys starting with '$' are comments - the loader ignores them.)
$outcome_note: outcome = the concrete result THIS audience needs from the content, in their world - not 'good content'. Write it as what changes for them when the piece works.
outcome: A floor associate can act on this in one short standing read, and re-teach it to a supervisor - so it gets adopted without a training session that will never be scheduled.
$thresholds_note: Verdict bars for THIS seat, applied to the 0-3 average: SHIP = good enough to ship; REVISE sits below it; a fatal criterion scored 0 forces REJECT regardless of the average. A forgiving audience can lower SHIP (e.g. 2.0); a demanding one can raise it. The dashboard reads these per seat.

criteria.$comment: A criterion = one bar that protects the outcome. 'the_bar' is the testable rule; 'protects_outcome' is why it matters for this reader; 'fatal': true means a 0 here forces REJECT whatever the average; 'anchors' define 0-3 concretely so two reviewers score alike; 'watch_for' is the plausible-looking failure that fools a generic reviewer; 'checks' wires a deterministic check (see checks.py) whose threshold comes from THIS card's args, never hardcoded.
criteria.the_bar: A distracted reader reaches the first useful action in the first two lines and finishes in under ~6 minutes standing up.
criteria.protects_outcome: If they can't act before the first interruption, they never come back - there is no session two.

anchors.0: No action reachable without a page of prose, or it assumes a desk and uninterrupted time.
anchors.1: Action exists but is buried past the fold, or needs re-reading.
anchors.2: Action is near the top and followable standing up.
anchors.3: First two lines say what it does for them; steps are doable one-handed, interrupted, on a phone.

criteria.watch_for: Well-written long-form. Fluency is not brevity; an 800-word explainer fails this for a reason a competence check never flags.

criteria.the_bar: Every instructed action is something this reader can do with the access they have.
criteria.protects_outcome: An instruction to open an admin center or install software isn't 'advanced' for this reader - it's impossible, so the whole piece stops working.

anchors.0: Requires admin rights, install, or budget the reader can never get.
anchors.1: Requires an approval or a person the reader has to go find.
anchors.2: Fully within the reader's standing access.
anchors.3: Explicitly names what needs the DM's sign-off and what doesn't.

criteria.watch_for: 'Reach out to your IT admin.' AC-01's store has no IT admin - that's a dead end, not a workaround.
